L208: ## NAME
L209: 
L210: git-update-ref - Update the object name stored in a ref safely
L211: 
L212: ## SYNOPSIS
L213: 
L214:     `git` `update-ref` [`-m` <reason>] [`--no-deref`] `-d` <ref> [<old-oid>]
L215:     `git` `update-ref` [`-m` <reason>] [`--no-deref`] [`--create-reflog`] <ref> <new-oid> [<old-oid>]
L216:     `git` `update-ref` [`-m` <reason>] [`--no-deref`] `--stdin` [`-z`] [`--batch-updates`]
L217: ## DESCRIPTION
L218: 
L219: Given two arguments, stores the <new-oid> in the <ref>, possibly dereferencing the symbolic refs. E.g. `git` `update-ref` `HEAD` <new-oid> updates the current branch head to the new object.
L220: Given three arguments, stores the <new-oid> in the <ref>, possibly dereferencing the symbolic refs, after verifying that the current value of the <ref> matches <old-oid>. E.g. `git` `update-ref` `refs/heads/master` <new-oid> <old-oid> updates the master branch head to <new-oid> only if its current value is <old-oid>. You can specify 40 "0" or an empty string as <old-oid> to make sure that the ref you are creating does not exist.
L221: The final arguments are object names; this command without any options does not support updating a symbolic ref to point to another ref (see cite117†git-symbolic-ref[1] ). But `git` `update-ref` `--stdin` does have the `symref-*` commands so that regular refs and symbolic refs can be committed in the same transaction.
L222: 
L223: If --no-deref is given, <ref> itself is overwritten, rather than the result of following the symbolic pointers.
L224: With `-d`, it deletes the named <ref> after verifying that it still contains <old-oid>.
L225: With `--stdin`, update-ref reads instructions from standard input and performs all modifications together. Specify commands of the form:
L226: 
L227:     update SP <ref> SP <new-oid> [SP <old-oid>] LF
L228:     create SP <ref> SP <new-oid> LF
L229:     delete SP <ref> [SP <old-oid>] LF
L230:     verify SP <ref> [SP <old-oid>] LF
L231:     symref-update SP <ref> SP <new-target> [SP (ref SP <old-target> | oid SP <old-oid>)] LF
L232:     symref-create SP <ref> SP <new-target> LF
L233:     symref-delete SP <ref> [SP <old-target>] LF
L234:     symref-verify SP <ref> [SP <old-target>] LF
L235:     option SP <opt> LF
L236:     start LF
L237:     prepare LF
L238:     commit LF
L239:     abort LF
L240: With `--create-reflog`, update-ref will create a reflog for each ref even if one would not ordinarily be created.
L241: With `--batch-updates`, update-ref executes the updates in a batch but allows individual updates to fail due to invalid or incorrect user input, applying only the successful updates. However, system-related errors—such as I/O failures or memory issues—will result in a full failure of all batched updates. Any failed updates will be reported in the following format:
L242: 
L243:     rejected SP (<old-oid> | <old-target>) SP (<new-oid> | <new-target>) SP <rejection-reason> LF
L244: Quote fields containing whitespace as if they were strings in C source code; i.e., surrounded by double-quotes and with backslash escapes. Use 40 "0" characters or the empty string to specify a zero value. To specify a missing value, omit the value and its preceding SP entirely.
L245: Alternatively, use `-z` to specify in NUL-terminated format, without quoting:
L246: 
L247:     update SP <ref> NUL <new-oid> NUL [<old-oid>] NUL
L248:     create SP <ref> NUL <new-oid> NUL
L249:     delete SP <ref> NUL [<old-oid>] NUL
L250:     verify SP <ref> NUL [<old-oid>] NUL
L251:     symref-update SP <ref> NUL <new-target> [NUL (ref NUL <old-target> | oid NUL <old-oid>)] NUL
L252:     symref-create SP <ref> NUL <new-target> NUL
L253:     symref-delete SP <ref> [NUL <old-target>] NUL
L254:     symref-verify SP <ref> [NUL <old-target>] NUL

L474:     Specifies one or more files to use for the user host key database, separated by whitespace. Each filename may use tilde notation to refer to the user's home directory, the tokens described in the cite7†TOKENS section and environment variables as described in the cite11†ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES section. A value of `none` causes cite3†ssh(1) to ignore any user-specific known hosts files. The default is ~/.ssh/known_hosts, ~/.ssh/known_hosts2.
L475: cite133†`VerifyHostKeyDNS` L476:     Specifies whether to verify the remote key using DNS and SSHFP resource records. If this option is set to `yes`, the client will implicitly trust keys that match a secure fingerprint from DNS. Insecure fingerprints will be handled as if this option was set to `ask`. If this option is set to `ask`, information on fingerprint match will be displayed, but the user will still need to confirm new host keys according to the `StrictHostKeyChecking` option. The default is `no`.
L477: See also cite81†VERIFYING HOST KEYS in cite3†ssh(1) .
L478: cite134†`VersionAddendum` L479:     Optionally specifies additional text to append to the SSH protocol banner sent by the client upon connection. The default is `none`.
L480: cite135†`VisualHostKey` L481:     If this flag is set to `yes`, an ASCII art representation of the remote host key fingerprint is printed in addition to the fingerprint string at login and for unknown host keys. If this flag is set to `no` (the default), no fingerprint strings are printed at login and only the fingerprint string will be printed for unknown host keys.
L482: cite136†`WarnWeakCrypto` L483:     controls whether the user is warned when the cryptographic algorithms negotiated for the connection are weak or otherwise recommended against. Warnings may be disabled by turning off a specific warning or by disabling all warnings. Warnings about connections that don't use a post-quantum key exchange may be disabled using the `no-pq-kex` flag. `no` will disable all warnings. The default, equivalent to `yes`, is to enable all warnings.
L484: cite137†`XAuthLocation` L485:     Specifies the full pathname of the cite59†xauth(1) program. The default is /usr/X11R6/bin/xauth.
L486: ## cite5†PATTERNS L487: 
L488: A cite138†pattern consists of zero or more non-whitespace characters, ‘*’ (a wildcard that matches zero or more characters), or ‘?’ (a wildcard that matches exactly one character). For example, to specify a set of declarations for any host in the ".co.uk" set of domains, the following pattern could be used:
L489: 
L490: `Host *.co.uk`
L491: 
L492: The following pattern would match any host in the 192.168.0.[0-9] network range:
L493: 
L494: `Host 192.168.0.?`
L495: A cite139†pattern-list is a comma-separated list of patterns. Patterns within pattern-lists may be negated by preceding them with an exclamation mark (‘!’). For example, to allow a key to be used from anywhere within an organization except from the "dialup" pool, the following entry (in authorized_keys) could be used:
L496: 
L497: `from="!*.dialup.example.com,*.example.com"`
L498: Note that a negated match will never produce a positive result by itself. For example, attempting to match "host3" against the following pattern-list will fail:
L499: 
L500: `from="!host1,!host2"`
L501: 
L502: The solution here is to include a term that will yield a positive match, such as a wildcard:
L503: 
L504: `from="!host1,!host2,*"`
L505: ## cite7†TOKENS L506: 
L507: Arguments to some keywords can make use of tokens, which are expanded at runtime. Tokens are expanded without quoting or escaping of shell characters. It is the user's responsibility to ensure they are safe in the context of their use.
L508: 
L509: The supported tokens in `ssh_config` are:
L510: %%
L511:     A literal ‘%’.
L512: %C
L513:     Hash of %l%h%p%r%j.
L514: %d
L515:     Local user's home directory.
L516: %f
L517:     The fingerprint of the server's host key.
L518: %H
L519:     The known_hosts hostname or address that is being searched for.
L520: %h
L521:     The remote hostname.
L522: %I
L523:     A string describing the reason for a `KnownHostsCommand` execution: either `ADDRESS` when looking up a host by address (only when `CheckHostIP` is enabled), `HOSTNAME` when searching by hostname, or `ORDER` when preparing the host key algorithm preference list to use for the destination host.
L524: %i
L525:     The local user ID.
L526: %j
L527:     The contents of the ProxyJump option, or the empty string if this option is unset.
L528: %K
L529:     The base64 encoded host key.
L530: %k
L531:     The host key alias if specified, otherwise the original remote hostname given on the command line.
L532: %L
L533:     The local hostname.
L534: %l
L535:     The local hostname, including the domain name.
L536: %n
L537:     The original remote hostname, as given on the command line.
L538: %p
L539:     The remote port.
L540: %r
L541:     The remote username.
L542: %T
L543:     The local cite128†tun(4) or cite140†tap(4) network interface assigned if tunnel forwarding was requested, or "NONE" otherwise.
L544: %t
L545:     The type of the server host key, e.g. `ssh-ed25519`.
L546: %u
L547:     The local username.
L548: `CertificateFile`, `ControlPath`, `IdentityAgent`, `IdentityFile`, `Include`, `KnownHostsCommand`, `LocalForward`, `Match exec`, `RemoteCommand`, `RemoteForward`, `RevokedHostKeys`, `UserKnownHostsFile` and `VersionAddendum` accept the tokens %%, %C, %d, %h, %i, %j, %k, %L, %l, %n, %p, %r, and %u.
L549: 
L550: `KnownHostsCommand` additionally accepts the tokens %f, %H, %I, %K and %t.
L551: 
L552: `Hostname` accepts the tokens %% and %h.
L553: 
L554: `LocalCommand` accepts all tokens.
L555: `ProxyCommand` and `ProxyJump` accept the tokens %%, %h, %n, %p, and %r.
L556: 
L557: Note that some of these directives build commands for execution via the shell. Because cite3†ssh(1) performs no filtering or escaping of characters that have special meaning in shell commands (e.g. quotes), it is the user's responsibility to ensure that the arguments passed to cite3†ssh(1) do not contain such characters and that tokens are appropriately quoted when used.

L20: /*
L21:  * This is to create corrupt objects for debugging and as such it
L22:  * needs to bypass the data conversion performed by, and the type
L23:  * limitation imposed by, index_fd() and its callees.
L24:  */
L25: static int hash_literally(struct object_id *oid, int fd, const char *type, unsigned flags)
L26: {
L27: 	struct strbuf buf = STRBUF_INIT;
L28: 	int ret;
L29: 	if (strbuf_read(&buf, fd, 4096) < 0)
L30: 		ret = -1;
L31: 	else
L32: 		ret = write_object_file_literally(buf.buf, buf.len, type, oid,
L33: 						 flags);
L34: 	close(fd);
L35: 	strbuf_release(&buf);
L36: 	return ret;
L37: }
L38: 
L39: static void hash_fd(int fd, const char *type, const char *path, unsigned flags,
L40: 		    int literally)
L41: {
L42: 	struct stat st;
L43: 	struct object_id oid;
L44: 	if (fstat(fd, &st) < 0 ||
L45: 	    (literally
L46: 	     ? hash_literally(&oid, fd, type, flags)
L47: 	     : index_fd(the_repository->index, &oid, fd, &st,
L48: 			type_from_string(type), path, flags)))
L49: 		die((flags & HASH_WRITE_OBJECT)
L50: 		    ? "Unable to add %s to database"
L51: 		    : "Unable to hash %s", path);
L52: 	printf("%s\n", oid_to_hex(&oid));
L53: 	maybe_flush_or_die(stdout, "hash to stdout");
L54: }
L55: static void hash_object(const char *path, const char *type, const char *vpath,
L56: 			unsigned flags, int literally)
L57: {
L58: 	int fd;
L59: 	fd = xopen(path, O_RDONLY);
L60: 	hash_fd(fd, type, vpath, flags, literally);
L61: }
L62: 
L63: static void hash_stdin_paths(const char *type, int no_filters, unsigned flags,
L64: 			     int literally)
L65: {
L66: 	struct strbuf buf = STRBUF_INIT;
L67: 	struct strbuf unquoted = STRBUF_INIT;
L68: 	while (strbuf_getline(&buf, stdin) != EOF) {
L69: 		if (buf.buf[0] == '"') {
L70: 			strbuf_reset(&unquoted);
L71: 			if (unquote_c_style(&unquoted, buf.buf, NULL))
L72: 				die("line is badly quoted");
L73: 			strbuf_swap(&buf, &unquoted);
L74: 		}
L75: 		hash_object(buf.buf, type, no_filters ? NULL : buf.buf, flags,
L76: 			    literally);
L77: 	}
L78: 	strbuf_release(&buf);
L79: 	strbuf_release(&unquoted);
L80: }
L81: int cmd_hash_object(int argc, const char **argv, const char *prefix)
L82: {
L83: 	static const char * const hash_object_usage[] = {
L84: 		N_("git hash-object [-t <type>] [-w] [--path=<file> | --no-filters]\n"
L85: 		   "                [--stdin [--literally]] [--] <file>..."),
L86: 		N_("git hash-object [-t <type>] [-w] --stdin-paths [--no-filters]"),
L87: 		NULL
L88: 	};
L89: 	const char *type = blob_type;
L90: 	int hashstdin = 0;
L91: 	int stdin_paths = 0;
L92: 	int no_filters = 0;
L93: 	int literally = 0;
L94: 	int nongit = 0;
L95: 	unsigned flags = HASH_FORMAT_CHECK;
L96: 	const char *vpath = NULL;
L97: 	char *vpath_free = NULL;
L98: 	const struct option hash_object_options[] = {
L99: 		OPT_STRING('t', NULL, &type, N_("type"), N_("object type")),
L100: 		OPT_BIT('w', NULL, &flags, N_("write the object into the object database"),
L101: 			HASH_WRITE_OBJECT),
L102: 		OPT_COUNTUP( 0 , "stdin", &hashstdin, N_("read the object from stdin")),
L103: 		OPT_BOOL( 0 , "stdin-paths", &stdin_paths, N_("read file names from stdin")),
L104: 		OPT_BOOL( 0 , "no-filters", &no_filters, N_("store file as is without filters")),
L105: 		OPT_BOOL( 0, "literally", &literally, N_("just hash any random garbage to create corrupt objects for debugging Git")),
L106: 		OPT_STRING( 0 , "path", &vpath, N_("file"), N_("process file as it were from this path")),
L107: 		OPT_END()
L108: 	};
L109: 	int i;
L110: 	const char *errstr = NULL;
L111: 	argc = parse_options(argc, argv, prefix, hash_object_options,
L112: 			     hash_object_usage, 0);
L113: 
L114: 	if (flags & HASH_WRITE_OBJECT)
L115: 		prefix = setup_git_directory();
L116: 	else
L117: 		prefix = setup_git_directory_gently(&nongit);
L118: 
L119: 	if (vpath && prefix) {
L120: 		vpath_free = prefix_filename(prefix, vpath);
L121: 		vpath = vpath_free;
L122: 	}
L123: 
L124: 	git_config(git_default_config, NULL);
L125: 	if (stdin_paths) {
L126: 		if (hashstdin)
L127: 			errstr = "Can't use --stdin-paths with --stdin";
L128: 		else if (argc)
L129: 			errstr = "Can't specify files with --stdin-paths";
L130: 		else if (vpath)
L131: 			errstr = "Can't use --stdin-paths with --path";
L132: 	}
L133: 	else {
L134: 		if (hashstdin > 1)
L135: 			errstr = "Multiple --stdin arguments are not supported";
L136: 		if (vpath && no_filters)
L137: 			errstr = "Can't use --path with --no-filters";
L138: 	}
L139: 
L140: 	if (errstr) {
L141: 		error("%s", errstr);
L142: 		usage_with_options(hash_object_usage, hash_object_options);
L143: 	}
L144: 	if (hashstdin)
L145: 		hash_fd(0, type, vpath, flags, literally);
L146: 
L147: 	for (i = 0 ; i < argc; i++) {
L148: 		const char *arg = argv[i];
L149: 		char *to_free = NULL;
L150: 
L151: 		if (prefix)
L152: 			arg = to_free = prefix_filename(prefix, arg);
L153: 		hash_object(arg, type, no_filters ? NULL : vpath ? vpath : arg,
L154: 			    flags, literally);
L155: 		free(to_free);
L156: 	}
L157: 
L158: 	if (stdin_paths)
L159: 		hash_stdin_paths(type, no_filters, flags, literally);
L160: 
L161: 	free(vpath_free);
L162: 
L163: 	return 0;
L164: }

L449: cite124†`SyslogFacility` L450:     Gives the facility code that is used when logging messages from cite3†ssh(1) . The possible values are: DAEMON, USER, AUTH, LOCAL0, LOCAL1, LOCAL2, LOCAL3, LOCAL4, LOCAL5, LOCAL6, LOCAL7. The default is USER.
L451: cite125†`TCPKeepAlive` L452:     Specifies whether the system should send TCP keepalive messages to the other side. If they are sent, death of the connection or crash of one of the machines will be properly noticed. However, this means that connections will die if the route is down temporarily, and some people find it annoying.
L453: The default is `yes` (to send TCP keepalive messages), and the client will notice if the network goes down or the remote host dies. This is important in scripts, and many users want it too.
L454: 
L455: To disable TCP keepalive messages, the value should be set to `no`. See also `ServerAliveInterval` for protocol-level keepalives.
L456: cite126†`Tag` L457:     Specify a configuration tag name that may be later used by a `Match` directive to select a block of configuration.
L458: cite127†`Tunnel` L459:     Request cite128†tun(4) device forwarding between the client and the server. The argument must be `yes`, `point-to-point` (layer 3), `ethernet` (layer 2), or `no` (the default). Specifying `yes` requests the default tunnel mode, which is `point-to-point`.
L460: cite129†`TunnelDevice` L461:     Specifies the cite128†tun(4) devices to open on the client (`local_tun`) and the server (`remote_tun`).
L462: The argument must be `local_tun`[:`remote_tun`]. The devices may be specified by numerical ID or the keyword `any`, which uses the next available tunnel device. If `remote_tun` is not specified, it defaults to `any`. The default is `any:any`.
L463: cite130†`UpdateHostKeys` L464:     Specifies whether cite3†ssh(1) should accept notifications of additional hostkeys from the server sent after authentication has completed and add them to `UserKnownHostsFile`. The argument must be `yes`, `no` or `ask`. This option allows learning alternate hostkeys for a server and supports graceful key rotation by allowing a server to send replacement public keys before old ones are removed.
L465: Additional hostkeys are only accepted if the key used to authenticate the host was already trusted or explicitly accepted by the user, the host was authenticated via `UserKnownHostsFile` (i.e. not `GlobalKnownHostsFile`) and the host was authenticated using a plain key and not a certificate.
L466: 
L467: `UpdateHostKeys` is enabled by default if the user has not overridden the default `UserKnownHostsFile` setting and has not enabled `VerifyHostKeyDNS`, otherwise `UpdateHostKeys` will be set to `no`.
L468: If `UpdateHostKeys` is set to `ask`, then the user is asked to confirm the modifications to the known_hosts file. Confirmation is currently incompatible with `ControlPersist`, and will be disabled if it is enabled.
L469: 
L470: Presently, only cite32†sshd(8) from OpenSSH 6.8 and greater support the "hostkeys@openssh.com" protocol extension used to inform the client of all the server's hostkeys.
L471: cite131†`User` L472:     Specifies the user to log in as. This can be useful when a different user name is used on different machines. This saves the trouble of having to remember to give the user name on the command line. Arguments to `User` may use the tokens described in the cite7†TOKENS section (with the exception of %r and %C) and environment variables as described in the cite11†ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES section.
L473: cite132†`UserKnownHostsFile` L474:     Specifies one or more files to use for the user host key database, separated by whitespace. Each filename may use tilde notation to refer to the user's home directory, the tokens described in the cite7†TOKENS section and environment variables as described in the cite11†ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES section. A value of `none` causes cite3†ssh(1) to ignore any user-specific known hosts files. The default is ~/.ssh/known_hosts, ~/.ssh/known_hosts2.
L475: cite133†`VerifyHostKeyDNS` L476:     Specifies whether to verify the remote key using DNS and SSHFP resource records. If this option is set to `yes`, the client will implicitly trust keys that match a secure fingerprint from DNS. Insecure fingerprints will be handled as if this option was set to `ask`. If this option is set to `ask`, information on fingerprint match will be displayed, but the user will still need to confirm new host keys according to the `StrictHostKeyChecking` option. The default is `no`.
L477: See also cite81†VERIFYING HOST KEYS in cite3†ssh(1) .
L478: cite134†`VersionAddendum` L479:     Optionally specifies additional text to append to the SSH protocol banner sent by the client upon connection. The default is `none`.
L480: cite135†`VisualHostKey` L481:     If this flag is set to `yes`, an ASCII art representation of the remote host key fingerprint is printed in addition to the fingerprint string at login and for unknown host keys. If this flag is set to `no` (the default), no fingerprint strings are printed at login and only the fingerprint string will be printed for unknown host keys.
L482: cite136†`WarnWeakCrypto` L483:     controls whether the user is warned when the cryptographic algorithms negotiated for the connection are weak or otherwise recommended against. Warnings may be disabled by turning off a specific warning or by disabling all warnings. Warnings about connections that don't use a post-quantum key exchange may be disabled using the `no-pq-kex` flag. `no` will disable all warnings. The default, equivalent to `yes`, is to enable all warnings.
L484: cite137†`XAuthLocation` L485:     Specifies the full pathname of the cite59†xauth(1) program. The default is /usr/X11R6/bin/xauth.
L486: ## cite5†PATTERNS L487: 
L488: A cite138†pattern consists of zero or more non-whitespace characters, ‘*’ (a wildcard that matches zero or more characters), or ‘?’ (a wildcard that matches exactly one character). For example, to specify a set of declarations for any host in the ".co.uk" set of domains, the following pattern could be used:
L489: 
L490: `Host *.co.uk`
L491: 
L492: The following pattern would match any host in the 192.168.0.[0-9] network range:
L493: 
L494: `Host 192.168.0.?`
L495: A cite139†pattern-list is a comma-separated list of patterns. Patterns within pattern-lists may be negated by preceding them with an exclamation mark (‘!’). For example, to allow a key to be used from anywhere within an organization except from the "dialup" pool, the following entry (in authorized_keys) could be used:
L496: 
L497: `from="!*.dialup.example.com,*.example.com"`
L498: Note that a negated match will never produce a positive result by itself. For example, attempting to match "host3" against the following pattern-list will fail:
L499: 
L500: `from="!host1,!host2"`
L501: 
L502: The solution here is to include a term that will yield a positive match, such as a wildcard:
L503: 
L504: `from="!host1,!host2,*"`
L505: ## cite7†TOKENS L506: 
L507: Arguments to some keywords can make use of tokens, which are expanded at runtime. Tokens are expanded without quoting or escaping of shell characters. It is the user's responsibility to ensure they are safe in the context of their use.
L508:
